oneSentence: Deployment means putting an AI system into real use so people or software can send it live inputs and receive live outputs.
plainExplanation:
A model can work well in a test notebook and still not be ready for real use. Deployment is the stage where that model is connected to the systems, devices or websites that people actually use. Inputs might be text from a form, an image from a camera, or rows from a database.

During deployment, the model runs on infrastructure such as a server or device. It may be embedded in an application or connected through an endpoint, a network address plus rules for exchanging requests and responses. Rules are also added for security, speed, logging and human oversight.

A deployed system must receive and check inputs, run the model, return outputs, and cope with failures or heavy traffic. Teams often watch latency, meaning delay, cost, and distribution shift, which means real-world data no longer looks like the data used earlier.

The result is a working service, not just a model file. Hosting covers the systems and services that keep the model available to receive requests, run and return outputs reliably and securely. Deployment is broader: it also includes workflow integration, controls, monitoring, updates and rollback.

everydayAnalogy.title: Putting a manifest checker onto the loading dock
everydayAnalogy.story: A shipping company tests a new tool that compares a delivery against its manifest. In the office, it works on sample lists. To use it at the loading dock, the team installs it on a tablet, connects it to the barcode scanner, sets who can use it, and decides what happens if the network fails. Once it is live, drivers scan boxes and the tool returns match, mismatch or needs human review in real time.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A manifest checker usually follows clearer rules than many AI systems. Real AI deployment can involve uncertain outputs, changing data patterns, scaling to many users, and version management. Also, some deployed systems keep learning offline and are updated later, while the tablet story sounds more fixed than that.

visual.title: From tested model to live service
visual.learningObjective: Show the main steps that turn a model from a tested artefact into a monitored service people or software can use safely.
visual.description: An ordered diagram with five boxes connected left to right. Read from a model that worked in testing to a live service that receives requests and is watched over time. Each box names one practical step in deployment rather than model training.

steps.label: 1. Start with a tested model
steps.explanation: A model has already been built and checked on test data, but it is not yet available in a real workflow.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a rectangle labelled 'Tested model' with a small file icon and a note 'works in testing'.

steps.label: 2. Place it on infrastructure
steps.explanation: The model is put on a server, cloud service or device with enough compute and storage to run it.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second rectangle labelled 'Run environment' with server or device icons; connect from step 1 with an arrow.

steps.label: 3. Connect inputs and outputs
steps.explanation: Forms, apps, databases or other software are linked to the model through an endpoint so requests can be sent and answers returned.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a third rectangle labelled 'Connected to workflow' with arrows in from an app/database icon and arrows out to a result panel.

steps.label: 4. Add controls
steps.explanation: The system gets authentication, rate limits, logging, fallbacks and, where needed, human review before action is taken.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a fourth rectangle labelled 'Controls and safeguards' with small shield, speedometer and human-check icons.

steps.label: 5. Go live and monitor
steps.explanation: Real users or systems start using it. Teams watch speed, failures, cost and changes in data so they can update or roll back if needed.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a fifth rectangle labelled 'Live service' with a small dashboard beneath showing latency, error rate and traffic.

visual.interaction: On click or keyboard focus, each step expands to reveal its explanation; a final toggle highlights the difference between 'hosting only' and 'full deployment'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains deployment as a five-step process. First, there is a tested model that works in evaluation but is not yet connected to real work. Second, it is placed on infrastructure such as a server, cloud service or device so it can run. Third, live inputs and outputs are connected through an endpoint, letting apps or other systems send requests and get results. Fourth, controls are added, including authentication, rate limits, logging, fallbacks and human review where needed. Fifth, the system goes live and is monitored for speed, failures, cost and changes in real-world data. The key message is that deployment means operationalising a model, not only storing it somewhere.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static five-box sequence shows the same process without animation: tested model, run environment, connected workflow, controls and safeguards, and live service with monitoring.

workedExample.scenario: An information management officer supporting conference services in Geneva must put a trained classifier into the facilities ticketing application before the next room-booking round opens. It will suggest whether each live request concerns room setup, building access, equipment or another issue, with service-desk staff confirming the label.
workedExample.input: New ticket text and existing non-sensitive routing fields from the approved ticketing system.
process: The officer packages the trained model with its software dependencies and installs it on approved production infrastructure.
The ticketing application sends each new request to an authenticated model endpoint and receives a suggested category.
Rate limits protect the service from traffic spikes, while failed or low-confidence requests fall back to the general queue.
Logs record response times, errors and model versions without retaining unnecessary ticket content.
Before each update, staff test the new version and keep the previous version available for rollback.
workedExample.result: The classifier now handles live requests inside the ticketing workflow. Staff retain the final routing decision, service performance is monitored, and requests continue to reach the general queue if the model is unavailable.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: At a shared services centre, a knowledge management officer is finalising the note for the file after a bilateral. The centre is deploying a model inside the approved records application to suggest metadata and access markings before the note is uploaded to the portal. The live service must return suggestions to the officer while leaving clearance and filing decisions with staff.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Deployment is the point at which the trained model meets the actual workflow. The release needs approved hosting, authenticated access, a connection to the records application, logging, monitoring, fallback behaviour and a tested way to restore the previous version if the update misbehaves.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: A note for the file may contain confidential or politically sensitive material. It must not be entered into an external or otherwise unapproved AI service. The production environment must be approved for the material concerned, access must be restricted and logged, and the officer must verify every suggested marking before clearance.

whyItMatters: For non-specialists, deployment is the point where an AI idea becomes an operational service with cost, risk and accountability. A model that looked impressive in testing can fail in practice if it is slow, expensive, insecure, hard to monitor or exposed to different data than expected. Decisions about deployment affect procurement, privacy, staffing, fallback procedures, user trust and whether humans stay in control. If you approve or use an AI system, you need to ask not only 'How accurate was it in testing?' but also 'Where will it run, who can access it, how will it be watched, and what happens when it is wrong or unavailable?'
whereYouMayHearIt: A vendor demo during a procurement meeting
An ICT governance board reviewing a production release
A go-live readiness meeting with the service owner
An incident review after a model endpoint fails
A change-control discussion before a model update

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a model scored well in testing, deploying it is just a technical formality.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Testing uses limited conditions. Real use adds messy inputs, traffic spikes, integration problems, user behaviour, security requirements and changing data. Deployment is where many practical failures appear, so operational planning matters as much as model quality.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Deployment and hosting mean the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Hosting usually refers to where the model runs. Deployment is wider. It includes connecting the model to real inputs and outputs, setting controls, monitoring behaviour, and managing updates or rollback if something goes wrong.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Once an AI system is deployed, it will keep working the same way.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Real-world conditions change. Users may send different kinds of inputs, organisations may change processes, and traffic may grow. A deployed system needs monitoring and maintenance because performance, cost and risk can shift over time.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Deployment is the step where an AI model stops being a test project and becomes a live tool that real people or software use.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Deployment is the operational release of a trained model into a production environment. It typically includes packaging the model and dependencies, provisioning compute, exposing an endpoint or embedding the model in an application, connecting live data flows, enforcing authentication and rate limits, enabling logging and observability, defining fallback behaviour and human review, and managing versioning, rollback and updates. In practice, deployment is about reliable inference under real conditions, not just whether the model can run once on a developer's machine.

keyTakeaway: A model is deployed only when it is connected to live work and operated as a service, with access controls, monitoring, human review, fallback and rollback.

quickCheck.question: Which description best matches deployment?
options: Saving a trained model file on a server for later use
Putting a model into a live workflow with connections, controls and monitoring
Collecting more training data so the model can improve
Running a model once on a laptop to see whether it works
quickCheck.explanation: Deployment is broader than storing or testing a model. It means making the model available in real use, linking it to inputs and outputs, adding operational controls, and monitoring what happens after it goes live.

issues.problem: “Live inputs” and “live outputs” can imply that deployment is limited to real-time services. Production deployment can also use scheduled or batch processing.
issues.fix: Deployment means putting an AI system into real use so it can process production inputs and provide outputs to people or software.

issues.problem: The second paragraph presents an endpoint as a required part of deployment, but a model can instead be embedded directly in an application or device. It also calls an endpoint merely “the place” requests are sent, omitting that it is a network address plus rules for a service function.
issues.fix: During deployment, the model runs on infrastructure such as a server or device. It may be embedded in an application or connected through an endpoint, a network address plus rules for exchanging requests and responses.

issues.problem: “Hosting is mainly where the model sits and runs” understates the separate definition of model hosting. Hosting also covers keeping the model available to receive requests and return outputs reliably and securely.
issues.fix: Hosting covers the systems and services that keep the model available to receive requests, run and return outputs reliably and securely. Deployment is broader: it also includes workflow integration, controls, monitoring, updates and rollback.

issues.problem: This step says forms, apps, databases or other software are linked through an endpoint, again treating an endpoint as mandatory. That contradicts the technical explanation, which correctly allows a model to be embedded in an application.
issues.fix: Forms, apps, databases or other software are linked through an endpoint or direct integration so inputs can be processed and results returned.

issues.problem: The correction reduces hosting to “where the model runs,” which blurs the supplied distinction by omitting availability, request handling, reliability and security.
issues.fix: Hosting covers systems and services that keep a model available to receive requests, run and return outputs reliably and securely. Deployment is wider, including workflow integration, controls, monitoring, updates and rollback.
